definition: Product appeal is the attractiveness of a product to consumers that can influence their likelihood of trying or choosing it. In the source, it is treated as a factor distinct from product quality and one that can affect market share, especially in the short term.

reasons: The packet does not define “product appeal” as consumer attractiveness or as influencing consumers’ likelihood of trying/choosing the product; it only refers to “appeal” in the context of a trade-off with quality in market dynamics.

Although the packet discusses a trade-off between “quality and appeal” and how market share responds over different time horizons, it does not explicitly state that appeal is treated as a distinct factor from quality (only that there is a trade-off).

The packet supports that time horizon changes the trade-off (short-term vs medium/long-term) and discusses effects on market share, but the claim that this is “especially in the short term” influencing trying/choosing is not directly supported in the supplied text.
The definition adds unsupported specifics such as consumer likelihood of trying or choosing a product; the packet only supports product appeal as a market parameter affecting market share.
The packet does support a contrast with product quality and mentions short- vs medium/long-term trade-offs, but it does not support the broader, consumer-behavior wording used here.
The field context is not clearly psychology/learning in the source; the packet is about trial-offer markets and marketing dynamics, so the sense should be tied more tightly to that usage.
